newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU "significantly closer" to gas deal.
newsitem.headline: EU "significantly closer" to gas deal.

text.p: European Union countries have moved significantly closer to reaching a deal to open up the EU gas market to competition, an EU official said on Wednesday.
The chances of EU energy ministers reaching a political agreement on partial liberalisation this year were "not at all negligible", the official told Reuters.

He said senior national energy officials meeting in Brussels on Tuesday had succeeded in narrowing the major differences between those EU states pushing for fast and far-reaching liberalisation and those who are more sceptical.

Tuesday's talks -- the first top level debate on a compromise deal proposed by the Dutch EU presidency -- focused on the extent to which national markets must open up, unbundling of accounts, control of supply and how to handle the long term take-or-pay contracts which dominate the EU's gas industry.

All 15 EU countries had agreed liberalisation was inevitable but long term take-or-pay contracts would remain a fact of life because of industry's concern about security of supply, so a formula had to be found for squaring the two, the official said.

The formula the national energy officials will put to their ministers, who next meet on May 26, will be for all EU states progressively to liberalise an agreed percentage of their gas markets over the next 10 years, though countries who so desire may introduce even more competition among domestic suppliers.

But if opening a domestic market causes a crisis for distributors locked into long-term take-or-pay contracts, then the national government will be able to appeal to the European Commission to let it temporarily limit newcomers' market access.

"We have to protect the viability of European (gas) companies," the EU official said, explaining that the introduction of competition could lure customers in search of better prices away from their traditional distributor, leaving the latter with a take-or-pay contract obliging him to pay for gas supplies he no longer needed.
The controversial question of how far liberalisation will go has been left for the ministers to solve, the EU official said.

The Dutch EU presidency had suggested as a first step that large industrial customers who consumed over 25 million cubic metres of gas a year should have the same rights as power generators to negotiate contracts directly with their suppliers.
Within 10 years, all final users consuming over a million cubic metres would become "eligible customers", according to the Dutch compromise.

But Tuesday's meeting rejected the idea of an EU-wide threshold and said different countries should be allowed to designate different eligible customers, so long as they achieved the same minimum degree of liberalisation.

Last December, EU energy ministers agreed to a similar formula for opening up the European electricity sector, obliging the member states to liberalise some 12 percent of their markets by 1999, rising to 33 percent by 2003.
Tuesday's meeting made better progress on unbundling of accounts and control of supply, the EU official said.
The member states had agreed gas undertakings should be obliged to file separate accounts for production, transmission, distribution, supply and storage.
And they had decided simply to monitor the gas market and react if a supply crisis loomed, rather than create a permanent mechanism to control supplies.
The EU relies on supplies from Russia, Algeria and Norway for 40 percent of its gas, with dependence on external supplies forecast to rise to 70 percent by 2020. -- Brussels Newsroom 32 2 287 6800
